newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan dollar ends at lowest level since 1988.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan dollar ends at lowest level since 1988.

text.p: The Taiwan dollar plunged further against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday, ending at its lowest level since 1988 on the greenback's persistent strength overseas and the central bank's lifting of a key defence, dealers said.
The local unit, facing intense selling pressure all session long, closed at T$28.480 against Tuesday's already sharply depreciated T$28.170 finish.
Turnover through dealers was active at US$344.5 million.

The central bank on Tuesday allowed the Taiwan dollar to fall below T$28 for the first time since 1989, opening a floodgate for local dollar selling amid the greenback's strength against the yen and other major currencies.
"The U.S. dollar continued to be strong (on Wednesday), and the central bank continued to let the market go. The result is another big fall," said one dealer at a foreign bank.

Dealers said that while the central bank for months had been permitting a slow descent for the local currency, its refusal to allow precipitous movements meant the Taiwan dollar actually has appreciated relative to the yen and other major currencies.
"As much as the Taiwan dollar has fallen, if you compare it to the yen, it may still be overvalued," said another dealer.

From early 1995 when the yen peaked against the U.S. dollar, the Japanese currency has depreciated some 47 percent against the greenback. In the same period, the Taiwan dollar has slid less than eight percent against the U.S. dollar -- even after Wednesday's big slide.

The Taiwan dollar's resulting rise against the yen has contributed to a ballooning of Taiwan's trade deficit with Japan as Taiwan's imports from Japan have become ever cheaper and its exports to Japan more expensive. In June, the imbalance rose 56.2 percent to US$1.524 billion compared to June 1996.
Dealers had predicted on Tuesday that Taiwan's dollar would drop to T$28.5 or even T$29 before seeing a rebound.
"The central bank seems very willing to stay clear of the market at this point," said the first dealer.
"But I don't think it will let the Taiwan dollar fall below T$28.5 as early as tomorrow," she added.
A T$28.20-50 range was seen for Thursday.

Dealers maintain that despite its tumble, the Taiwan dollar clearly was not suffering from -- or vulnerable to -- the kind of speculative attacks that have shocked several southeast Asian currencies in July, particularly the Thai baht.

While those countries' currencies fell precipitously despite strident public opposition by their central banks, Taiwan's central bank has been seen by experts as tacitly welcoming, even encouraging, a well-tempered depreciation in the interest of stronger exports -- Taiwan's economic life-blood.
They say Taiwan's central bank, boasting imposing foreign exchange reserves of over US$90 billion, could easily defend the currency as it often has at times of political uncertainty.

The bank's strength was never clearer during a long stretch in 1995-96 when it held the Taiwan dollar above T$27.5 despite military intimidation by rival China that triggered a run on foreign exchange and gold and a flood of capital outflows.
Within two months after that crisis passed, the central bank said it was no longer defending T$27.5, setting the currency onto a long, languid depreciation that has yet to play out.
